column2: How many times can I coach the same person for CIPS credit?
column5:
A maximum of six sessions with the same individual count toward your CIPS total.

You are welcome to keep coaching someone beyond six if it genuinely helps them. Nobody will stop you, and nobody should. Only the first six add credit.

Why the limit exists

The cap is there to keep CIPS doing their job. Competency Improvement Practice Sessions are meant to build your competence across a range of different people with different goals, which is what real practice looks like once you are working professionally.

If most of your sessions were with one person, you would get very good at coaching that person. You would learn their patterns, their vocabulary, what works with them. What you would not learn is the thing CIPS exist to teach: how to be useful to someone you have never met, whose situation you do not yet understand, in the first twenty minutes.

The six-session limit also spreads the available coaching across more of the people applying through the Get Free Coaching board, which matters, because those are members of the public receiving genuine help at no cost.

At the senior levels, where CIPS requirements rise to 24 sessions, that breadth is exactly what the requirement is measuring.

column2: How do I offer free coaching to someone outside Achology?
column5:
Through the Get Free Coaching board, where people outside the community browse and apply for complimentary one-to-one sessions offered by members. Each session you host counts as 1 CIPS credit, and this becomes part of your requirements from Senior Achologist I onward.

How the board works

Unlike VALTS, these are not scheduled calendar events. You make sessions available on the board, and someone outside the community, facing a real challenge or working toward something they actually want, applies for one.

That difference is the entire point. You are coaching a person who wants help, not a peer who understands the exercise. No shared vocabulary, no allowance made for the fact that you are practising. Just someone with a problem and an hour of your attention.

Most members find their first one nerve-racking and their fifth one genuinely enjoyable, which is roughly the intended trajectory.

What counts toward credit

Each session hosted earns 1 CIPS credit, and up to six sessions with the same individual count toward your total. Your claims are verified by SoMAP before they are added to your record.

If you are on the receiving side of this, and wondering whether the free coaching is genuine, it is, and you can find it at free coaching.

column2: Who is responsible for verifying my Achology CPD claims?
column5:
Every CPD claim you make is verified by SoMAP, the Society of Modern Applied Psychology, an independent accreditation body that operates separately from Achology's commercial side by design. Nothing you self-report reaches your official record without passing through it. That independence is the entire point: it is what lets your record mean something to anyone outside Achology.

How the verification actually works

The pipeline is straightforward, and deliberately not instant. You complete an activity, whether attending a VALTS session, delivering coaching, or offering a session to someone outside the community, and you submit a claim. SoMAP committee members, all of them Master Achologists, then review each submission independently. Only once a claim is verified is it committed to your official record, which is held in the Achology Member Data Centre and tracks your activity across every member level. Your personal progress checklist is a planning tool; the verified record is the one that counts.

Why the independence matters

A professional development record is only worth as much as the process behind it. If Achology simply accepted whatever members reported about themselves, the record would be a list of claims, possibly accurate, with no way for anyone outside to know. A client choosing a coach, an employer reviewing a candidate, an organisation deciding whether a qualification means anything: none of them can audit your honesty directly. What they can rely on is that somebody qualified and independent already did. That is why the check exists, and why the short delay between submitting a claim and seeing it appear is the process doing its job, not a system running slowly.

What sits alongside it

Verification is one of two things that make Achology's training checkable from outside. The other is UK Register of Learning Providers registration, which lists Achology as a registered provider of learning. Together they mean an Achology standing rests on a registered provider plus independent verification behind every level, both of which you can check without taking anyone's word for it.

What verification produces

Two kinds of certificate come out of this. Completing a course earns a certificate of completion. Reaching a verified member level on the pathway earns a certificate of achievement, which is the one that carries weight with a client or employer, precisely because an independent body stood behind it. If someone needs to confirm your standing, how an Achology certificate is verified explains the check from their side.

column2: Is my personal progress checklist considered part of my CPD record?
column5:
No. Your checklist is a planning tool. Your CPD record is the official one, and it contains only what SoMAP has independently verified.

The difference

The checklist is yours. It shows what you have done and what is still outstanding for the next member level, and it is genuinely useful for keeping track. But it carries no standing on its own. Ticking a box does not move you anywhere.

The official record, held in the Achology Member Data Centre, contains only verified activity. Something appears there once it has been submitted as a claim and confirmed.

Where this catches people out

The gap between the two is where members occasionally get a surprise: work completed, checklist looking healthy, and then a level does not arrive because the underlying claims were never submitted.

So the habit is simple. Treat the checklist as your plan and the verified record as your score, and submit claims as you go rather than saving them up. Doing the activity is most of the work; submitting it is what turns it into progress.

If you need to show your record to someone else, how to evidence your CPD and learning progression covers that.

column2: Is it necessary to redo the Code of Ethics training annually?
column5:
Yes, from Achologist Adept onward. You attend the live Code of Ethics training once within every 12 months, at every level from Adept up to and including Master Achologist maintenance. It is not required for the first step from Member to Achologist.

How often it runs

Quarterly, giving four opportunities a year to meet a once-a-year requirement. You need only one. Attendance is verified by SoMAP and updated in your record.

Why annually rather than once

Because ethics is not a topic you complete.

The Code of Ethics sets the standards of professional conduct expected of every practising Achologist, and it is treated as something you return to and practise, not a document read once and filed. The reason for repeating it is straightforward: the people who come to you for help deserve a practitioner who has actively thought about what ethical practice means recently, not someone who considered it once, years ago, before they had ever sat with a real client.

It is also true that ethical questions get harder with experience, not easier. The dilemmas troubling a practitioner in their fifth year are not the ones covered in their first. Returning annually is what keeps the training useful rather than ceremonial.

The Code of Ethics is one of three separate codes at Achology, and it is easy to confuse them.

column2: How do a certificate of completion and a certificate of achievement differ?
column5:
They record two different kinds of thing. A certificate of completion says you finished a course. A certificate of achievement says you reached a verified member level on the CPD pathway.

The certificate of completion

You receive one when you complete a course. It confirms you worked through the material and finished it. That is a real milestone and worth having.

The certificate of achievement

This one is not tied to a single course. As you meet the cumulative requirements for a member level and SoMAP verifies each claim, your progression is recognised with a certificate of achievement.

What each says to an employer

Picture the two on a CV. A completion certificate tells an employer you studied a subject and finished the course, which is genuinely worth stating.

An achievement certificate tells them something stronger: that you reached a standard of practice an independent body checked and stood behind. One describes study; the other describes verified competence, and only one of them is hard for a candidate to overstate.

Which one matters to whom

If you are learning for yourself, completion certificates may be all you ever need. If you intend to practise, the achievement certificate is the one that carries weight, precisely because someone other than you confirmed it.

It is also the difference between completing a course and being competent, which is worth reading if you are weighing up what a certificate is for. For what your certificate proves to a third party, see what an Achology certificate actually proves.

column2: Is Achology listed on the UK Register of Learning Providers?
column5:
Yes. Achology is registered on the UK Register of Learning Providers (UKRLP), with the Provider Reference Number (PRN) 10099815. The UKRLP is the official record of learning providers in the United Kingdom, and the Provider Reference Number is the unique identifier for Achology on it. You can check it yourself, without taking our word for it.

How to check it

The UKRLP maintains a public provider lookup. Searching the register for the Provider Reference Number 10099815, or for the Achology name, returns the registered provider entry. That is the point of a public register: anyone assessing Achology can confirm the registration directly at source, rather than relying on a claim made on this page.

What the registration does, and does not, mean

It is worth being precise here, because this is an area where training providers are often vague, and we would rather be plain. Being on the UK Register of Learning Providers means Achology is a registered provider of learning, identifiable by its Provider Reference Number. It does not mean any individual course is a regulated or statutory qualification. If the question behind your question is how an Achology certificate compares to a formal academic award, how Achology certificates compare to university psychology degrees answers it directly and honestly.

What sits alongside it

The registration is one of two things that make Achology's training checkable from outside. The other is SoMAP, the Society of Modern Applied Psychology, the independent body that reviews and confirms every professional development claim, found at thesomap.org. What gives an Achology standing its credibility is the combination: a registered provider, plus independent verification behind every member's level. Both are checkable, and Achology's accreditation position is set out in full separately.

column2: What is the Achology Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC)?
column5:
The Code of Character and Conduct, or CCaC, is Achology's character-development code. It sets out nine virtues, each worked through in its own live session, and its purpose is plainly stated in the handbook itself: not a set of rules, but a shared commitment to the community's growth. It is the character strand of the CPD (continuing professional development) pathway, trained and tracked alongside the ethics strand.

How it is built

The CCaC runs as ten live sessions: an introduction, then one session for each of the nine virtues, which are Courage, Temperance, Justice, Wisdom, Magnificence, Magnanimity, Friendliness, Truthfulness, and Wittiness. It rests on Aristotle's virtue ethics: the idea that character is not something you are born with, but something developed through deliberate practice, and that each virtue is a balanced middle point between two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency.

What a virtue session is actually like

A CCaC session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the session is really an honest examination of where you sit on that virtue's spectrum. Courage, for example, is the point between recklessness and cowardice, and the session asks you to look at which way you tend to lean, in the company of other members doing the same. That shared honesty is the method: character, in this view, is built by examining it openly, over time, with people who will be straight with you.

Where it sits on the pathway, and why

You complete all ten sessions before you move from Achologist to Achologist Adept, then keep eight of the ten current within any rolling 12-month period. The CCaC is one of three separate codes: distinct from the Code of Ethics, which governs professional practice, and the Community Code of Conduct, which governs behaviour on the community platform. It exists because most training develops only what you can do. The CCaC is how Achology also attends to who you are becoming while you learn, on the plain view that a capable practitioner with poor character helps no one.

column2: What are Achology's 9 Code of Character and Conduct virtues?
column5:
The nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) are Courage, Temperance, Justice, Wisdom, Magnificence, Magnanimity, Friendliness, Truthfulness, and Wittiness. Each is explored in its own live session, and together with an introductory session they make up the ten CCaC sessions on the CPD (continuing professional development) pathway.

How the virtues are understood

The nine are drawn from Aristotle's virtue ethics, where each virtue is a balanced middle point between two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage, for instance, is the point between recklessness and cowardice. Each session works through its virtue with a set of reflection questions, so you examine where you actually sit on that spectrum rather than reading a definition and moving on.

Why these nine, and why in sessions

The virtues are treated as qualities you develop through practice, not traits you either have or lack. Working through them in the company of other members, over time, is how the CCaC builds character alongside the professional skill the rest of the pathway develops. Holding 8 of the 10 sessions current is what keeps that work live, rather than something completed once and forgotten.

column2: How do the Code of Ethics, CCaC, and Community Code of Conduct differ?
column5:
Achology has three separate codes, and they are easy to confuse. The Code of Ethics governs professional practice, the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) develops character, and the Community Code of Conduct sets the rules for behaviour on the community platform.

What each one is

  • The Code of Ethics, formally the Ethical Framework for Practitioners of Applied Psychology, sets the standards of professional conduct expected of every practising Achologist. Annual training in it is a CPD (continuing professional development) requirement from Achologist Adept onward.
  • The CCaC is the character-development code: nine virtues trained through ten live sessions, forming the character strand of the pathway.
  • The Community Code of Conduct is the separate set of rules for the Circle community platform, governing how members behave in that shared space.

One situation, three codes

It helps to see them at work on a single moment. Imagine you are coaching another member in a live session, and something sensitive comes up.

The Code of Ethics governs how you handle that professionally: confidentiality, competence, the client's interests. The CCaC is the character behind it: the honesty and humility you bring to the room. The Community Code of Conduct covers how you then conduct yourself in the group afterwards, in the shared space.

A simple way to hold the difference

The Code of Ethics is about how you practise with clients. The CCaC is about who you are becoming as a person. The Community Code of Conduct is about how you treat other members day to day.

Two of the three, the Code of Ethics and the CCaC, are trained and tracked on the CPD pathway; the third simply governs conduct in the community space.

column2: How many CCaC sessions do I need to complete, and how often?
column5:
There are ten Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) sessions in total: an introduction, plus one for each of the nine virtues. You complete all ten before you progress from Achologist to Achologist Adept. After that, you keep 8 of the 10 current within any rolling 12-month period to stay compliant.

What "keeping them current" means

The 8-of-10 requirement is ongoing, not a one-time hurdle. Sessions run regularly through the year, and because compliance is measured over a rolling 12 months, sessions gradually drop out of the window as time passes. Leaving too long a gap is where members find themselves falling short.

Why it works this way

Character, in the CCaC's view, is built by examining virtues honestly, in good company, over time, not by finishing a course once and moving on. The rolling requirement keeps that examination live. Holding 8 of 10 current is also what keeps your status at green, which is required for CPD (continuing professional development) progression at every level from Achologist Adept upward.

column2: What do the green and red CCaC statuses indicate?
column5:
Green and red are the two states of your Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) compliance. Green means at least 8 of your 10 CCaC sessions are current within the rolling 12-month period, which is what CPD (continuing professional development) progression requires. Red means fewer than 8 are current, and while you are red, your progression on the pathway is paused until you restore it.

How you move between them

Because compliance is measured over a rolling 12 months, sessions drop out of the window as time passes, so staying green takes consistent engagement rather than a single burst. If your current sessions fall below eight, your status turns red. Attending enough sessions to bring the count back to eight or more returns you to green.

Why it matters

Green status is a condition for progressing at every level from Achologist Adept upward, sitting alongside the annual Code of Ethics training as the two ongoing compliance requirements. Red does not erase anything you have already earned; it holds your progression in place until your compliance is restored. That is the system's way of keeping the character strand a live commitment rather than a box ticked once.

column2: Why does Achology's character code draw from Aristotle?
column5:
Achology's character code, the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC), is built on Aristotle's virtue ethics because that tradition treats character as something you develop, not something you are simply born with or without. For a learning community whose whole premise is that people are capable of growth, a framework built on deliberate practice is a natural fit.

What virtue ethics actually says

If the phrase is new to you, the idea behind it is refreshingly plain. Most ethical systems ask "what are the rules, and did you follow them". Virtue ethics asks a different question: "what kind of person are you becoming".

Its answer is that good character is grown, through practice and honest effort, the same way any skill is. You are not born courageous or patient; you become so by acting that way, repeatedly, until it holds.

The idea of the middle point

Aristotle's particular contribution is that each virtue sits as a balanced mean between two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between recklessness and cowardice; generosity between wastefulness and meanness.

The CCaC takes nine of these virtues and works through each in its own session, asking you to examine honestly which way you tend to lean.

Why it suits Achology

This character-first approach matches how Achology treats ethics more widely: the aim is to help members aspire to become better, not simply to follow rules. Virtue ethics gives the CCaC a way to develop character over time, through honest self-examination in the company of other members, which is exactly how the sessions are designed to run.

column2: What are the five principles of Achology's community?
column5:
Achology's five community principles set the behavioural benchmark for the learning community. They are Respect and Inclusivity, Active Engagement, Integrity and Professionalism, Ethical Conduct, and Shared Responsibility. They come from the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) and describe how members treat one another and the space they share.

What each one means

  • Respect and Inclusivity: diversity enriches the community, every perspective is valued, and respect is treated as the cornerstone of growth.
  • Active Engagement: learning is a shared effort, so members take part, listen with intention, ask thoughtful questions, and give constructive feedback.
  • Integrity and Professionalism: trust is built through consistent honesty, accountability, and professionalism, including upholding confidentiality.
  • Ethical Conduct: members respect others' rights, follow applicable laws, and contribute in ways aligned with the community's standards.
  • Shared Responsibility: the community is a collective effort, so issues are addressed collaboratively rather than left to fester.

What they look like in practice

These are not abstractions once you are inside the community. Active Engagement is the member who reads a coaching post properly and gives a considered reply, rather than a one-line reaction.

Shared Responsibility is the group addressing a difficult thread openly and kindly, instead of letting it sour. Integrity is a member holding a confidence they were trusted with. The principles describe the ordinary conduct that keeps a large learning community worth being part of.

How they are held

The five principles are part of the CCaC, and they sit alongside the nine virtues the code trains: the virtues describe the character to develop, the principles describe how to conduct yourself with others. They also connect to Achology's wider ten value commitments and nine value-based principles.

column2: What are the suggested character traits of an Achologist?
column5:
The Achology Code of Ethics names 22 character traits as the essential personal and moral qualities of an Achologist. They are grounded in a smaller set of moral foundations, honesty, integrity, kindness, fairness, respect, responsibility, and empathy, with trust treated as the cornerstone of every professional relationship. The traits describe who an Achologist is expected to be, alongside what they agree to do.

The 22 traits

In full, they are: Alertness, Attentiveness, Availability, Cautiousness, Compassion, Cooperation, Courage, Diligence, Discipline, Empathy, Enthusiasm, Flexibility, Generosity, Honesty, Humility, Initiative, Integrity, Orderliness, Patience, Positivity, Resilience, and Wisdom.

How they are used

These 22 are an aspirational inventory: qualities to grow toward and examine honestly in yourself, rather than a checklist you pass. They overlap with the nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC), which shares some of the same ground, but the two are distinct instruments. The CCaC virtues are trained and tracked through live sessions; these 22 traits are aspired to and self-examined. Together with the commitments every practising Achologist makes, they paint the full picture of the person the framework is helping you become.

column2: What is the Achology Code of Ethics (Ethical Conduct)?
column5:
The Achology Code of Ethics is the framework of professional conduct that every practising Achologist works within. Its formal name is the Ethical Framework for Practitioners of Applied Psychology. It is the primary reference members use when making decisions about their own conduct, whether professional, relational, financial, or social, and adhering to it is a condition of standing as a member.

What it is grounded in

The framework is built on virtue ethics, the tradition running from Socrates and the Stoics through Aristotle, which emphasises cultivating good character over simply following rules. The handbook presents the code as an integrity health check rather than a box-ticking exercise, with the aim of helping members aspire to be better, not merely to do the right thing in the moment. Integrity is named its cornerstone virtue.

The three ways it is used

The code is not a document you read once and shelve. The handbook names three live uses for it: guiding everyday professional practice, including being open about it with a client at the outset; supporting ethical decision-making, giving you a structured way to weigh a real dilemma when two principles pull against each other; and supporting reflection, explicitly including the coaching and practice sessions on the pathway. In other words, it is meant to be used in the room, not admired on a shelf.

How it is trained and kept current

The code comes with a six-part video training course, working through moral and ethical excellence, the role of an ethically minded Achologist, the integrity health check, ongoing character development, the qualities that positively influence people, and a closing commitment to keep the practice alive. Attending the live Code of Ethics training once a year is a CPD compliance requirement from Achologist Adept onward. It is one of Achology's three conduct codes, distinct from the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) and the Community Code of Conduct. Its values are expressed in more usable form as the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles.

column2: What are the ten core value commitments of Achology?
column5:
Achology's ten value commitments are the beliefs its Code of Ethics commits the organisation and its members to. They shape the goals Achology sets and the decisions it makes.

The ten commitments

  • Upholding human rights, individuality, and dignity for all.
  • Actively supporting people in relieving personal suffering and distress.
  • Promoting the wellbeing, personal growth, and capabilities of individuals.
  • Enhancing the quality of relationships between people, built on trust and understanding.
  • Strengthening personal resilience and effectiveness.
  • Encouraging people to embody virtuous and ethical characteristics in their interactions.
  • Maintaining the confidentiality of people's private information, prioritising their safety and wellbeing.
  • Upholding the integrity of the practitioner and client relationship in applied psychology.
  • Enhancing the usefulness of abstract psychological knowledge in practical, everyday applications.
  • Ensuring equitable and affordable access to training in applied psychology.

Where you actually see them

A list of values is only worth as much as its visibility, so it is worth pointing to where these show up. The confidentiality commitment is the root of Achology's privacy promises across its policies.

The applied-knowledge commitment is why the whole platform is built around practice rather than theory alone. And the access commitment is behind the free-to-read Knowledge Hub and the affordability of the training.

How they fit the wider framework

The ten commitments work alongside the nine value-based principles, which turn these values into a method for real decisions, and the five community principles, which express them in daily conduct. Together they say the same thing in three registers: what Achology believes, how it decides, and how members behave.

column2: What are Achology's nine value-based principles?
column5:
Achology's nine value-based principles are the way its Code of Ethics turns its values into something a member can act on. The handbook's own reasoning is that articulating values as principles brings clarity and makes them usable when a real decision has to be made.

The nine principles

  • Personal Integrity: living consistently by core principles such as honesty, fairness, and decency.
  • Personal Autonomy: staying true to yourself and your own principles, free from external manipulation.
  • Unconditional Inclusion: accepting every person's full contribution, regardless of difference.
  • Altruism: serving the needs of others above personal interest, with empathy as its engine.
  • Moral Imagination: the ability to envision several options for resolving an ethical dilemma.
  • Growth Mindset: treating skills as learnable and failures as opportunities to learn.
  • Social Contribution: prioritising giving over taking within families, neighbourhoods, and communities.
  • Personal Responsibility: taking ownership and acting as a role model whose influence reaches beyond you.
  • Maturity in Character: self-awareness, social awareness, and the wisdom to learn from experience.

How they guide a real decision

The handbook gives a simple test for using them. If one or more of these principles is strongly reflected in a decision, without contradicting any other, the decision can be regarded as ethically well-founded.

Say a client shares something that worries you. Personal Integrity and Altruism both point toward acting in their interest; Unconditional Inclusion and Personal Autonomy remind you to respect their right to decide for themselves.

Where the principles cannot all be honoured at once, you weigh which matter most. That weighing is the skill.

Why this matters

That test is what turns the ten value commitments from a statement into a working method, and it connects directly to the seven marks of maturity the framework describes.

column2: What are the seven signs of maturity that Achology teaches?
column5:
Achology's seven marks of maturity come from the Code of Ethics, in a section on the essence of maturity. They describe a mature person as someone whose decisions are rooted in values rather than in passing emotions or opinions. The marks give members a picture of the character the whole framework is trying to help them grow toward.

The seven marks

  • Keeps long-term commitments, delaying gratification and honouring commitments even when they are uninspiring.
  • Is indifferent to flattery or criticism, holding a secure identity that is not shaken by external opinion.
  • Possesses a spirit of humility, honouring others and acknowledging their contributions.
  • Makes decisions based on character, acting proactively rather than looking for excuses.
  • Can prioritise self last, contributing to others' wellbeing in a balanced, discerning way.
  • Seeks wisdom before acting, keeping a teachable spirit and valuing counsel from the wise.
  • Consistently expresses gratitude.

How to read them

The marks are best read as a description to grow into rather than a test to pass. They line up closely with the nine value-based principles, where Maturity in Character is itself named, and with the framework's wider belief that character, more than circumstances, is what carries a person through difficulty. That belief is also why Achology emphasises character development alongside professional skill.

column2: What are my commitments as a practising Achologist?
column5:
As a practising Achologist who serves the public, you commit to five ethical standards toward your clients: you put the client's needs first, work to a high standard and within your competence, keep your professional relationships healthy and honouring, and protect confidentiality. These come from the Achology Code of Ethics, and meeting them is a condition of standing as a member.

The five commitments

  • Always put the client's needs first, ahead of your own interests.
  • Work to a high standard, keeping your professional development current so your practice stays sharp.
  • Work within your competencies, and be honest about them in relation to a client's situation.
  • Maintain healthy, honouring relationships, held with unconditional positive regard, authenticity, and empathy.
  • Maintain confidentiality, privacy, and trust, never disclosing a client's information without consent or genuine necessity.

What sits alongside them

The code adds a few practical duties. When you offer services to the public, you make sure appropriate insurance is in place, and you hold the same standards whether you work online or in person. You are also expected to be accountable, ready to explain how you have met your obligations. All of it exists to protect the client's interests and their capacity to decide for themselves.

These commitments build on the character traits expected of an Achologist, and they apply with added care while you are still training: see the standards for a trainee Achologist.

column2: Which professional standards apply to a trainee Achologist?
column5:
Trainee Achologists, members still working through a practitioner qualification course, hold to the same ethical framework as qualified members, with a few added responsibilities that reflect where they are. The central one is honesty about their status: a trainee tells clients, or makes sure they know, that they are training.

What trainees commit to

  • Tell clients you are a trainee. After qualifying, whether to disclose past trainee status becomes a matter of professional judgement.
  • Get permission before using any client work for educational purposes, with identities thoroughly anonymised, and treat consent as mandatory wherever anonymity cannot be guaranteed.
  • Provide services that meet the framework's professional, moral, and ethical standards.
  • Work with reasonable care and skill, collaborating with senior practitioners and professional advisors.
  • Stay mindful of any conflict between obligations, such as to other clients or a training provider, and seek guidance.
  • Talk honestly with trusted members of the community about your training, client work, and ethical practice.

Why the extra care

These standards protect the people a trainee works with while the trainee is still developing. Being open about trainee status, careful with client material, and willing to seek guidance is treated not as a limitation but as part of practising ethically from the start. They sit on top of the commitments every practising Achologist makes and the character traits the community expects.

column2: Is there a free Achology membership tier, and what does it include?
column5:
Yes, Achology has a free membership tier, and it needs no payment to join. It is a real membership with genuine access, not a preview screen: you get free events through the week, the coaching board, the discussion forum, and the quarterly live Code of Ethics training. It exists to let you experience the community properly before deciding whether to pay for more.

What the free membership includes

  • The events calendar, with free events running Monday to Friday, excluding holidays.
  • The coaching board, where you can apply for one-to-one coaching sessions offered by subscribing members.
  • The discussion forum, where you can ask questions of SoMAP (the Society of Modern Applied Psychology) members and the Achology Eldership.
  • The quarterly live Code of Ethics training.

What your first week can look like

You can join a free event, post to the coaching board and apply for a session, and start reading and asking in the forum, all without paying anything. That is enough to answer the real question most people have at this stage, which is not "what are the features" but "are these my kind of people, and is this worth my time". The free tier is built to let you find that out honestly.

What it does not include, and why

The free tier does not include the courses, the unlimited live sessions, or the structured mentorship, and that is deliberate rather than mean. Those sit with paid Achology Membership, at $7 for the first 30 days and then $34.50 a month. The free tier also does two useful jobs at once: it gives subscribing members people to practise their coaching and tutorials with, which feeds the accreditation pathway, and it lets you try the community before committing. The fuller cost picture is in How much does Achology cost?

column2: How do monthly and annual Achology memberships differ?
column5:
The difference between monthly and annual Achology Membership is how you pay and how much you save. Monthly is $7 for your first 30 days, then $34.50 a month, billed each month until you cancel. Annual is $345 for a full year, paid once. Both give you exactly the same access to the community; the only thing that changes is the commitment and the cost.

What each one costs

  • Monthly: $7 for the first 30 days, then $34.50 per month, cancellable at any time to stop future payments.
  • Annual: $345 per year, which works out at roughly two months free compared with paying monthly for a year, and renews annually unless you cancel before the renewal date.

What that access actually contains

Whichever plan you choose, membership is where the practising side of Achology happens: access to courses, unlimited live sessions, structured mentorship, the coaching board, daily discussion groups, and the networking that runs through it all. It is the difference between owning a course and taking part in a community, which is worth being clear about before you choose a plan: membership and courses are not the same purchase.

Which one to choose

The monthly plan, with its $7 first month, is the low-commitment way in: sensible if you want to try the community or are not yet sure how long you will stay. The annual plan is the better value if you already know you want to be part of Achology for the year, since it saves you about two months' worth of payments. One honest point either way: membership is non-refundable once your access starts, because that access begins immediately, though you can cancel at any time to stop future payments. So if you are unsure, the monthly trial is the gentler place to begin, and the free tier is gentler still.

column2: My course included free membership. What happens when it ends?
column5:
When you buy a course, it comes with three months of complimentary Achology Membership. When those three months end, the membership does not simply stop: it continues automatically at the standard monthly rate of $34.50 a month until you cancel it. You can cancel at any time inside the community platform, Circle, which stops all future payments.

What you need to do

If you want to keep your community access, you do not need to do anything: it carries on and you are billed monthly once the complimentary period is over. If you do not want it to continue, cancel it before the three months end, and you will not be charged. Cancelling stops future payments; it does not remove the course you bought, which remains yours to access.

A couple of things worth knowing

The complimentary period is longer with some purchases: the Access All Areas Pass includes twelve months of membership rather than three. And membership is non-refundable once access has started, so if you decide it is not for you, the thing to do is cancel to stop future payments rather than expect a refund of a month already begun. If you refund the course itself, the membership is handled separately.

column2: If I request a refund on a course, will I lose my free membership?
column5:
No. Refunding a course does not, by itself, cancel the complimentary Achology Membership that came with it. The two are handled separately, so if you refund a course within the 14-day money-back guarantee and you also do not want the membership to continue, you need to cancel the membership yourself.

How to cancel the membership

You cancel the membership inside the community platform, Circle, which stops all future payments. It takes a moment, and it is worth doing at the same time as your refund request so the membership does not quietly continue and start billing at $34.50 a month once the complimentary period ends.

The wider refund position

Courses, bundles, and the Access All Areas Pass carry a full 14-day money-back guarantee, no reason required; how to request a refund walks through the steps. Membership itself is different: it is non-refundable once your access has started, because that access begins immediately, but you can cancel it at any time to stop future payments. So the clean way to step away fully is to request your course refund and cancel the membership separately.

column2: What is the total number of courses offered by Achology?
column5:
Achology offers 28 individual courses in total, grouped into seven schools of applied psychology, each school gathering the courses that belong to one field. They range from short, focused masterclasses of ten to sixteen hours up to full practitioner diploma courses, so the catalogue holds both a first taste of a subject and a complete professional training in it.

How the 28 are organised

The seven schools are the School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), the School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP), the School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping, the School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology, the School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW), the School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience, and the School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD). Because some subjects genuinely belong to more than one field, a single course can sit in more than one school, so the schools' totals add up to more than 28.

The clearest example is the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), the foundational course that appears in all seven.

Where to start among 28

Twenty-eight is a lot to face at once, so most people do not choose a course so much as choose a direction. If you are new, the three learning paths are the simplest way in, grouping the catalogue by goal rather than by subject.

If you already know the field you want, each school bundle collects its courses in one place. And the foundational diploma, DiMAP, is where a great many members begin, because it underpins the rest.

Ways to buy them

You can take a course on its own, buy a whole school as a bundle, or take the Access All Areas Pass, which includes all 28 courses. Whichever route you choose, the courses themselves are identical; the difference is only how many you gain access to at once, and the fuller cost picture sets out what each option costs.

column2: What courses are part of each Achology school bundle?
column5:
Each of Achology's seven schools is a bundle of courses in one field. Six of the schools hold five or six courses; the School of Personal Growth and Development holds twelve. The Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) is shared across all seven, because it is the foundational course the whole catalogue builds on.

A note on the figures below: because some courses appear in more than one school, the student totals count those shared courses under each school, so they overlap rather than sum.

The seven schools and their courses

  • School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), 5 courses, 162+ hours: DiMAP, A Beginner's Guide to Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) Practitioner Training, Neuro-Linguistic Programming Master Practitioner Course, and Mindset Mastery.
  • School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP), 5 courses, 121+ hours: DiMAP, The CBT Toolkit, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) Practitioner Course, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness, and The Strategic Goal Setting and Action Planning Masterclass.
  • School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping, 6 courses, 150+ hours: DiMAP, Life Coaching Certificate Course (Beginner to Advanced), Life Coaching Blueprint, The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan), Skilled Helper Practitioner Course (Advanced to Expert), and The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass.
  • School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology, 5 courses, 145+ hours: DiMAP, Hypnotherapy Practitioner Course, Counselling Skills Practitioner Course, The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan), and The Communication Skills and Social Intelligence Masterclass.
  • School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW), 5 courses, 121+ hours: DiMAP, Mindfulness Practitioner Diploma Course, Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace, Mindfulness for Highly Efficient Management and Leadership, and The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass.
  • School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience, 5 courses, 131+ hours: DiMAP, Mental Health and Wellbeing Practitioner Diploma Course, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness, Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace, and Mindset Mastery.
  • School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD), 12 courses, 183+ hours: DiMAP plus eleven personal-development courses spanning self-belief, confidence, emotional intelligence, clarity and purpose, goal setting, communication, productivity, mental toughness, relationships, leadership-focused mindfulness, and entrepreneurship.

Buying a school

Each school bundle includes its courses plus twelve months of Achology Membership, and works out cheaper than buying the same courses separately.

If you want everything, the Access All Areas Pass includes all 28 courses across all seven schools.

column2: Are there Achology courses that are included in multiple bundles?
column5:
Yes. Several courses are shared across more than one school bundle, because some subjects genuinely belong to more than one field. The clearest example is the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), which appears in all seven schools as the foundational course the rest build on.

The shared courses

  • Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP): in all seven schools.
  • Mindset Mastery: The Ultimate NLP-Based Guide to Self-Discovery: in the NLP school and the Mental Health school.
  • Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness: in the CBP school and the Mental Health school.
  • The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan): in the Life Coaching school and the Person-Centred school.
  • Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace: in the Mindfulness school and the Mental Health school.
  • Mindfulness for Highly Efficient Management and Leadership: in the Mindfulness school and the Personal Growth school.
  • The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass: in the Life Coaching, Mindfulness, and Personal Growth schools.
  • The Strategic Goal Setting and Action Planning Masterclass: in the CBP school and the Personal Growth school.
  • The Communication Skills and Social Intelligence Masterclass: in the Person-Centred school and the Personal Growth school.

What this means when you buy

If you buy more than one school, you may find a shared course appears in both, and you do not lose out: you keep lifetime access to the course either way. It simply reflects that these subjects are useful across fields. If you would rather have everything without tracking the overlaps, the Access All Areas Pass includes all 28 courses once.

column2: What are the three learning paths offered by Achology?
column5:
Achology groups its courses into three high-level learning paths, a simpler way to find your direction than working through all 28 courses one by one. They are Mental Health and Wellbeing, Personal Growth and Development, and Applied Psychology Certification. Some courses sit in more than one path, because the same learning can serve more than one goal.

What each path is for

  • Mental Health and Wellbeing: courses focused on understanding and supporting mental health, resilience, and emotional wellbeing, both for yourself and for the people you help.
  • Personal Growth and Development: courses focused on confidence, communication, clarity, productivity, and personal effectiveness, for people who want to grow in their own lives and work.
  • Applied Psychology Certification: the Practitioner Certification courses that are required for CPD (continuing professional development) progression toward Achologist status and beyond.

How to choose between them

The honest way to use the paths is to start from why you are here, not from the course list. If your aim is professional practice and accreditation, the Applied Psychology Certification path holds the courses the pathway actually counts, so that is where to look first.

If you want to support your own or others' mental health, the Mental Health and Wellbeing path points you at the courses built for that. If your aim is personal growth in your work and relationships, the Personal Growth path is the one.

Someone training to coach professionally and someone wanting to steady their own life will pick different starting points, and the paths exist to make that first choice obvious.

How paths relate to schools

The paths and the seven schools are two views of the same catalogue. A path groups courses by the goal you are pursuing; a school groups them by subject.

They are a way of choosing where to start, not fixed tracks you are locked into, and you are free to take courses from more than one path. If you would rather not choose at all, the school bundles and the Access All Areas option give you whole groups at once.

column2: What does the DiMAP course upgrade include?
column5:
The DiMAP Course Upgrade is a bundle that pairs the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) with twelve months of Achology Membership, for $399. It is an upgrade on buying the diploma by itself, which is $299 and comes with three months of complimentary membership. So the real question the upgrade answers is not "which course" but "how long do I want to be part of the community while I study it".

What DiMAP itself is

DiMAP is Achology's flagship course and the foundation the rest of the catalogue builds on: it appears in all seven schools and runs to more than fifty hours of material. It is also the course the CPD pathway requires by Senior Achologist I, so for anyone heading toward accreditation, it is not optional. That is why it is the course most often bought first, and the one the upgrade is built around.

What you get for the difference

For $100 more than the course alone, the upgrade extends your community membership from three months to a full twelve. That is the whole of the difference, and it is worth seeing plainly: membership on its own is $34.50 a month, so nine extra months bought this way is straightforward value if you are going to use them.

Membership is where the practising side of the pathway happens, the live events, the coaching board, the mentorship groups, and the community the CPD pathway runs through.

Who it suits, and who it does not

The upgrade suits someone who already knows they want to stay engaged with the community for the year and work toward accreditation: for them, the twelve included months are better value than paying month to month once the complimentary period ends.

It suits you less well if you mainly want the diploma itself and are not yet sure about the community. In that case the standard course, with its three complimentary months, lets you try the community before committing to a year, and you keep lifetime access to the course either way.

column2: Which Achology events qualify for accreditation credit?
column5:
Nine of Achology's 22 event types earn accreditation credit. These are the events governed by SoMAP, the Society of Modern Applied Psychology, the independent body that verifies members' professional development.

The other 13, the general community events and mentorship groups, are valuable for learning and connection, but carry no credit in any role. That is worth knowing before you plan a year around them.

The six that earn VALTS or PALS credit

  • Skill Development Workshop
  • Principle-Based Reflective Discussion
  • Case Study-Based Discussion Group
  • The Coaching HOT Seat
  • Achologist-Led Tutorial
  • Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback Session

Attending one earns a VALTS credit; hosting or taking a coaching role earns a PALS credit.

The three that count differently

The remaining three accrediting events serve your record in other ways:

  • The Code of Ethics Training and the Code of Character and Conduct Training earn no VALTS or PALS credit. Instead, attending keeps your two compliance strands current, which is required for progression at all.
  • The Group Facilitation and VALTS Host Training is the gateway event: completing it qualifies you to host, and therefore to earn PALS that way.

Every credit and compliance record is verified by SoMAP before it counts. If you are unsure which events suit where you currently are, choosing the right event for your level is the practical guide.

column2: What steps should I follow to organise my own Achology event?
column5:
Once you reach Achologist level and complete the Group Facilitation and VALTS Host Training, you can host five credit-earning event types with no further approval: the Skill Development Workshop, the Principle-Based Reflective Discussion, the Case Study-Based Discussion Group, the Coaching HOT Seat, and the Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback session.

Hosting an Achologist-Led Tutorial requires Achologist Adept, and a few events are hosted only by the Eldership team.

The six steps to publish one

Every event uses a locked template, so each one reads consistently regardless of who is hosting. The only part you write yourself is a short Theme of This Specific Event paragraph naming what your session covers.

1. Open the Host a Live Event space on Circle and find your event in the Event Descriptions Library.

2. Copy the full template.

3. Start a direct message to a member of the Eldership team.

4. Paste the template into the message.

5. Write your Theme of This Specific Event paragraph at the top.

6. Send it. The Eldership member approves it, publishes it, and adds the event image.

That is genuinely the whole process. The template exists so that hosting your first event is a matter of describing your theme rather than designing a session from nothing.

Hosting community events

The community events, the ones carrying no credit, sit in a second tier reached by informal invitation from the Eldership team rather than application. Readiness is recognised through sustained participation in the facilitation mentorship group and the host training. Once invited, you publish them the same way.

Remember that hosting earns you a PALS credit, and that you still submit the claim afterwards like any other activity. Whether members can host their own workshops is covered separately for anyone still deciding.

column2: What is the process for submitting a CPD claim after participating?
column5:
After you host or attend a credit-earning event, you submit a claim through the member self-report form. You are also invited to record a short takeaway from the session while still on the group call. SoMAP, the Society of Modern Applied Psychology, then reviews the claim and records the credit against your account.

When the credit is confirmed

Not the moment you submit it. Hosts will not tell you your credit has been recorded until verification is complete, and that step is not instant.

This is deliberate, and worth understanding rather than finding frustrating. No self-reported activity enters your official record until an independent body has checked it, which is precisely what makes the record credible to anyone outside Achology. A record that updated instantly would be a record nobody had checked.

Where the verified credit lives

Once verified, the credit is added to your official record in the Achology Member Data Centre, which tracks activity across every member level.

Your own progress checklist is a useful planning tool, but it is not the official record: only verified claims count toward progression. The practical habit is to submit as you go rather than saving up a term's worth of activity, because unsubmitted work is invisible to the system no matter how much of it you have done.

column2: What does the Coaching HOT Seat entail?
column5:
The Coaching HOT Seat is one of the six VALTS (Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions) types, and it is a live coaching demonstration. One member takes the seat with a real challenge or goal, up to three Achologists coach them in turn, and the rest of the group observes.

What actually happens in it

The person in the seat brings something genuine they are working through, not a tidy example invented for practice. The coaching then happens in real time, in front of everyone.

That is what makes it valuable and slightly daunting in equal measure. For the observers, watching skilled coaching up close, and seeing how a good coach handles a real person, is one of the fastest ways to improve their own practice.

Up to three Achologists coach in turn, so you also see different styles brought to the same problem, and how each reads the person in front of them slightly differently.

What it is like to sit in the seat

Taking the seat yourself is the part members are often nervous about and glad they did. You bring a real issue and receive focused coaching from several practitioners, with the group's attention on the work rather than on you.

Most people find it far more supportive than exposing, and leave with something they can actually use.

How credit works

The roles earn different credit. The coaches earn a PALS (Peer-Peer Applied Learning Sessions) credit for coaching, the person in the seat earns a PALS received, and the observers earn a VALTS credit for attending.

Why members rate it

Coaching in public asks a different quality of performance than a private session: you cannot hide a hesitation, and you see how others handle the same moment. That is why the HOT Seat is one of the alternative PALS formats required at the senior levels, and why many members point to it as where their coaching genuinely sharpened. Once qualified, you can host your own, and it counts among the events that earn accreditation credit.

column2: With which Achology company am I formally contracting?
column5:
Achology is a trading name, and which company you are actually contracting with depends on what you bought and when. For courses and course bundles, and for community subscriptions bought on or after 1 June 2023, the company is Achology Transactions Ltd (ATL). For community subscriptions bought before 1 June 2023, it is the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd (AMAP).

The simple version

  • Courses and course bundles: Achology Transactions Ltd.
  • Community subscriptions bought on or after 1 June 2023: Achology Transactions Ltd.
  • Community subscriptions bought before 1 June 2023: the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd.

Where to find the details

Both companies are registered in Scotland and share the same registered office in Glasgow. If you need the company numbers and the registered address, for an invoice, a records request, or formal correspondence, those are set out in the registered company details. If your question is really about a purchase, the refund policy and how refunds are requested apply the same way whichever company holds your contract.

column2: What are the major milestones in Achology's history?
column5:
Achology's story begins in 2012, when Kain Ramsay published what is described as the world's first video-based psychology course. The learning platform itself was founded in 2014, and the original company, the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology, was founded in 2017.

From there it grew into a global applied-psychology platform with more than 670,000 students in its database today. The milestones below are less a list of dates than a single, consistent direction: from one course, toward a global, accredited, community-based way of learning.

The milestones along the way

  • 2012: the world's first video-based psychology course is published, the foundation of what became Achology.
  • 2014: the Achology learning platform is founded, with 12 courses.
  • 2015: the curriculum expands to 17 interlinked courses.
  • 2016: live online skill and competency development workshops begin, the first sign of the community model to come.
  • 2017: a landmark year, reaching 100,000 students, with a bespoke platform build begun and the exclusive Skilled Helper course launched with Prof. Gerard Egan.
  • 2019: the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), the flagship course, launches.
  • 2020: the shift to online learning accelerates worldwide, and the platform meets the demand at scale.
  • 2021: the community learning system is upgraded and gains CPD (continuing professional development) accreditation, with 350,000 total enrolled students.
  • 2022: half a million students reached worldwide, with the curriculum grown to 25 courses.
  • 2023: the version 2 community portal launches with the current 28-course curriculum.
  • 2024: the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) is founded by Master Achologists, to raise integrity standards in the field.
  • 2025: a full migration to Circle gives Achology its permanent online home.
  • 2025 to 2026: an Eldership team is established and free learning is opened to the public, with 670,000+ students in the database.

How to read the dates

It is worth separating two threads that often get muddled. The brand's public story begins in 2012 with that first course, while the founding of the original company was 2017. An older claim that Achology was founded in 2015 is simply incorrect, and we would rather say so than let it stand.

What actually runs through the whole timeline is one consistent move: from selling single courses, toward accreditation, community, and now free public learning through the Knowledge Hub. The fullest picture of where that arrived is in What is Achology?

column2: What exactly is the Achology Knowledge Hub?
column5:
The Achology Knowledge Hub is Achology's free library of applied-psychology learning content, found at the /learn/ section of the site. It brings together several kinds of content in one place, organised so you can find your way around by topic rather than having to know exactly what you are looking for.

What it holds

The Hub gathers five types of content: articles, book notes, quotes, workbooks, and author biographies. Everything is organised into seven categories, Psychology, Helping People, Mental Wellness, Motivation, Personal Growth, General Interest, and Wisdom for Life, and cross-linked with a set of tags so you can browse by the outcome you want, the problem you are facing, or the approach you want to learn.

How it differs from Help

The Knowledge Hub is for learning, and it is separate from the Help section you are reading now, which answers support and pre-purchase questions. The two are kept apart on purpose, because someone exploring a topic and someone resolving a support issue are looking for different things. The Hub also has its own search bar for finding content across all its categories. It is entirely free to read; what Achology charges for is its courses and its community membership, which go deeper than any library can.

column2: Is the Achology Knowledge Hub available for free to read?
column5:
Yes. The Achology Knowledge Hub is free to read. Its articles, quotes, and book notes are public pages, open to anyone, with no membership or payment required. The downloadable workbooks are also free, provided in exchange for an email address rather than a fee.

What is free and what is paid

What Achology charges for is its courses, its school bundles, and its community membership, not the Knowledge Hub. The Hub is meant to be genuinely useful on its own: you can read as much of it as you like without paying. If a piece of content leads you toward a course that goes deeper on the same subject, that is an invitation, not a wall.

Why it is free

Making this learning openly available fits Achology's commitment to affordable, equitable access to applied psychology. The Knowledge Hub is the part of the site anyone can benefit from immediately, whether or not they ever buy a course or join the community.
